**How to Quantify the Number of Mitochondria Per Cell** Below you’ll find a practical “cook‑book” style guide covering everything from why you’d want to do this, through sample handling, imaging modalities, data extraction, and basic troubleshooting. Feel free to skip sections that don’t apply to your system – most labs only need one or two of the approaches listed. --- ### 1️⃣ Why Count Mitochondria? | Question | Typical Answer | |----------|----------------| | **What does it tell us?** | Cellular energy status, metabolic reprogramming, apoptosis susceptibility, disease phenotypes (mitochondrial disorders, cancer). | | **When is it useful?** | Comparing wild‑type vs mutant lines, drug screens, aging studies, stem‑cell differentiation assays. | > *Tip:* Decide early whether you care about total numbers, density (per µm²), volume fraction, or functional readouts (membrane potential, ROS production). Your choice will dictate the best method below. --- ### 2️⃣ Overview of Available Techniques | Technique | Strengths | Weaknesses | Ideal Use Case | |-----------|------------|-------------|---------------| | **Fluorescence Microscopy (widefield / confocal)**
(MitoTracker®, TMRE, Mitotracker Green, GFP‑tagged proteins) | Fast, live‑cell compatible, good throughput | Limited depth, diffraction limit (~200 nm lateral) | Quick screen, sub‑population analyses | | **Super‑Resolution Fluorescence** (STED, SIM, Airyscan) | ~50–100 nm resolution | Requires specialized optics, more expensive | Detailed morphology, cristae structure | | **Transmission EM** (TEM/SEM) | Ultimate structural detail (<1 nm) | Laborious, low throughput, fixed samples | Gold standard for absolute counts | | **Flow Cytometry** (with mitochondrial dyes) | Thousands of events/min, quantitative | No spatial info, requires dissociation | Population statistics, viability tests | | **High‑Content Screening Platforms** (automated microscopes + AI) | Large datasets, reproducible | Setup cost, training required | Drug discovery, multi‑parameter profiling | | **Image Analysis Pipelines** (Fiji/ImageJ, CellProfiler, Ilastik) | Customizable, open source | Needs validation, may misclassify artifacts | Any imaging modality once raw data acquired | --- ### 3️⃣ Practical Protocols #### A. Fluorescent Staining & Widefield Imaging ```text Materials --------- • Cells plated at 30–70% confluency on #1.5 glass coverslips • MitoTracker™ Red CMXRos (or green variant) • PBS, DPBS • Paraformaldehyde (PFA) 4% • DAPI (optional) Procedure ---------- 1. Wash cells twice with warm HBSS/PBS. 2. Incubate with 250 nM MitoTracker® Red diluted in complete media for 20 min at 37°C. 3. Remove stain, wash gently with fresh media/HBSS. 4. Fix with 4% PFA for 15 min (if not doing live imaging). 5. Optional: counterstain nuclei with DAPI (300 ng/mL, 5 min). 6. Mount coverslip onto slide with ProLong Diamond antifade mounting medium. ``` *Imaging Settings* | Parameter | Suggested Value | |-----------|------------------| | Objective | 60× oil immersion (NA ≥ 1.4) | | Exposure time | < 500 ms (avoid bleaching) | | Z‑stack spacing | ≤ 0.3 μm (to capture entire nuclear envelope) | | Pixel size | 80 nm/pixel (Nyquist sampling) | #### B. Confocal Reconstruction & Segmentation (Fiji Macro) ```javascript // Simple macro to segment mitochondria and compute mean particle count per cell. // Assumes bright‑field nuclei stained with DAPI. // Load stack open("path/to/image.tiff"); // Split into color channels run("Split Channels"); selectWindow("C01"); // DAPI rename("Nuclei"); selectWindow("C02"); // MitoTracker rename("Mitotifs"); // Threshold nuclei setAutoThreshold("Default dark"); // Convert to binary mask run("Convert to Mask", ""); run("Analyze Particles...", "size=50-Infinity circularity=0.00-1.00 show=Masks display clear add"); // Label each nucleus run("Watershed"); roiManager("Add"); // For each nucleus, measure mitochondria inside for(i=0;i *Note*: This macro assumes all mitochondria lie within the same focal plane as the nucleus. For thicker samples, consider generating maximum projections before segmentation. #### C. Transmission EM Absolute Counting 1. **Fixation**: 2.5% glutaraldehyde in cacodylate buffer, 1 h at RT → post-fix in 1% osmium tetroxide, 45 min. 2. **Dehydration**: graded ethanol series → propylene oxide. 3. **Embedding**: Epon resin, polymerize overnight at 60 °C. 4. **Sectioning**: Ultrathin (60–90 nm) sections cut on ultramicrotome. 5. **Staining**: Uranyl acetate (25 min) → lead citrate (5 min). 6. **Imaging**: TEM at 120 kV, magnifications 4000x–8000x. 7. **Counting Strategy**: - Randomly pick fields ensuring >10 cells per field. - Manually trace mitochondria boundaries or use semi‑automatic edge detection. - Record number per cell; calculate average ± SD. > *Pitfall*: Overlap between adjacent mitochondria can inflate counts—use serial section tomography if precision matters. #### D. Flow Cytometric Estimation ```python import pandas as pd from flowkit import FlowKit # Acquire data with BD FACSCanto II data_file = "sample.fcs" flow_data = FlowKit(data_file) # Gate singlets, exclude debris singlet_gate = flow_data.singlets() live_cells = flow_data.viability().exclude() # Measure median fluorescence of MitoTracker median_mt = flow_data.median('FITC-A') # adjust channel accordingly print(f"Median MitoTracker FITC-A: {median_mt}") ``` > *Interpretation*: Higher median fluorescence correlates with greater mitochondrial mass but doesn’t give discrete counts unless combined with calibration beads or volumetric standards. --- ### 4️⃣ Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them | Issue | Cause | Remedy | |-------|------|--------| | **Photobleaching** | Long exposure times, intense illumination | Reduce laser power, shorten dwell time, use anti‑bleach reagents | | **Overlapping Signals** | Dense packing, thick specimens | Deconvolution, optical sectioning, super‑resolution | | **Non‑specific Dye Binding** | Membrane depolarization, dead cells | Include controls (FCCP treatment), pre‑incubate with inhibitors | | **Segmentation Errors** | Variable brightness, noise | Apply adaptive thresholds, morphological opening/closing | | **Cell Size Variation** | Different cell cycle stages | Normalize counts to surface area or DNA content | | **Batch Effects** | Day‑to‑day variation | Run internal standards, randomise plate layout | --- ### 5️⃣ Tips for Robust Quantitation 1. **Use Multiple Replicates** – At least three biological repeats plus technical duplicates. 2. **Validate Against Ground Truth** – Cross‑check fluorescence counts against EM counts in a subset of samples. 3. **Automate Where Possible** – Scripts reduce human bias; however always manually inspect a few cases. 4. **Document Every Step** – Keep detailed SOP logs (media composition, incubation times, microscope settings). 5. **Statistical Rigor** – Report means ± SEM, perform appropriate t-tests or ANOVA depending on design. --- ### 6️⃣ Resources & Further Reading | Resource | Link | |---------|-----| | **MITO Tracker Handbook** | https://www.biorad.com/en-us/shop/product/MITOTRACKER-RED-CMXROS | | **EM Atlas of Human Organelle Morphology** | https://ematlas.org | | **CellProfiler Documentation** | https://cellprofiler.readout.io/docs/latest/index.html | | **Open Source Super‑Res Toolkit** | https://github.com/johnsonlab/superres-tools | | **Review Article** | *Quantifying Mitochondrial Dynamics Using Live‑Cell Imaging*, Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 2019 | --- ### 🎯 Bottom Line - **Fastest & Most Accessible:** Fluorescent widefield/confocal + Fiji segmentation. - **Gold Standard for Accuracy:** Serial-section TEM with manual counting. - **Throughput‑Driven Screens:** Automated high‑content imaging coupled with ML segmentation. - **Population Statistics:** Flow cytometry gives bulk estimates quickly. Pick the approach that balances accuracy, speed, and resources for your specific question. Happy counting!
